marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q001.takeaway: The umbilical dermatome is T10, corresponding to the tenth thoracic spinal nerve.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q001.displayText:
The umbilical dermatome is T10, corresponding to the tenth thoracic spinal nerve.

The marked dermatome which includes the umbilicus is supplied by T10.

The dermatomal distribution of the abdominal region is: T7-T9 supply skin from the xiphoid process to just above the umbilicus; T10 supplies skin around the umbilicus; T11-T12 supply skin below the umbilicus up to the suprapubic region; L1 supplies skin around the genitalia and upper medial thigh.
emphasis: The umbilical dermatome is T10, corresponding to the tenth thoracic spinal nerve

rationales.a: T8 is above the umbilical dermatome.
rationales.b: T9 is superior to the usual umbilical sensory level.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q002.takeaway: Inferior vena caval obstruction produces lower abdominal wall collateral flow ascending or rerouting toward the SVC; the described pattern is IVC obstruction.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q002.displayText:
Inferior vena caval obstruction produces lower abdominal wall collateral flow ascending or rerouting toward the SVC; the described pattern is IVC obstruction.

The pattern of subcutaneous venous circulation depicted in the image can be seen in cases of inferior vena caval obstruction.

The level of the umbilicus is a watershed area for venous and lymphatic circulation. The systemic veins anastomose with tributaries of portal veins at the umbilicus. Normally, venous blood and lymphatics flow upwards above the plane of the umbilicus and downwards below this plane.

The source figure contrasts portal hypertension (radiating away from the umbilicus like a star/caput medusae), inferior vena caval obstruction, superior vena caval obstruction, and portal obstruction.
emphasis: Inferior vena caval obstruction produces lower abdominal wall collateral flow ascending or rerouting toward the SVC; the described pattern is IVC obstruction

rationales.a: SVC obstruction produces upper-body venous congestion and downward thoracoabdominal collateral flow.
rationales.c: SMV obstruction affects portal venous drainage rather than superficial abdominal wall venous return.
rationales.d: Budd–Chiari obstructs hepatic venous outflow and causes portal hypertension/ascites, not this collateral pattern.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q003.takeaway: A midline laparotomy passes through linea alba and fascia but avoids the transversus abdominis muscle.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q003.displayText:
A midline laparotomy passes through linea alba and fascia but avoids the transversus abdominis muscle.

The image shows a midline incision used for emergency laparotomy. Transversus abdominis muscle is not incised in this approach.

Layers pierced in the midline approach, superficial to deep: skin; superficial fascia (Camper's and Scarpa); linea alba; transversalis fascia; extraperitoneal fat; parietal peritoneum. There are no muscles pierced in this approach.

Layers pierced in a flank approach, superficial to deep: skin; superficial fascia (Camper's and Scarpa); external oblique; internal oblique; transversus abdominis; transversalis fascia; extraperitoneal fat; parietal peritoneum.

Clinical note: umbilical and epigastric hernia can occur due to a congenital or acquired defect in the linea alba such as a midline abdominal incision.
emphasis: A midline laparotomy passes through linea alba and fascia but avoids the transversus abdominis muscle

rationales.a: Transversalis fascia is traversed in a midline incision.
rationales.b: Extraperitoneal fat lies deep to transversalis fascia and is pierced.
rationales.c: Skin and superficial fascia, including Camper and Scarpa layers, are incised.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q004.takeaway: Lateral trunk flexion uses ipsilateral external and internal oblique muscles together.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q004.displayText:
Lateral trunk flexion uses ipsilateral external and internal oblique muscles together.

The given image shows lateral flexion of the trunk being performed, which is done by the ipsilateral external oblique (EO) and internal oblique (IO) muscles.

The anterior abdominal wall comprises four muscles: external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, and rectus abdominis.

Movements: forward flexion of the trunk (lumbar spine) — rectus abdominis and bilateral IO and EO; lateral flexion — ipsilateral IO and EO; rotation — ipsilateral IO and contralateral EO; pulling the testes towards the superficial inguinal ring — cremaster.
emphasis: Lateral trunk flexion uses ipsilateral external and internal oblique muscles together

rationales.a: Rectus abdominis flexes the trunk forward rather than producing isolated lateral flexion.
rationales.b: Contralateral internal oblique pairs with ipsilateral external oblique in trunk rotation.
rationales.d: Transversus abdominis and internal oblique do not form the principal lateral-flexion pair.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q005.takeaway: A transversus abdominis plane block deposits anesthetic between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, where nerves course.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q005.displayText:
A transversus abdominis plane block deposits anesthetic between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, where nerves course.

The local anesthetic is injected between the internal oblique (marked 2) and transversus abdominis (marked 3) muscles in the anterior abdominal wall because the neurovascular plane lies between these muscles.

The plane contains the lower six thoracic nerves, iliohypogastric nerve, posterior intercostal and subcostal vessels, and anastomosis between superior and inferior epigastric arteries.

The transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is a regional anesthetic technique used for abdominal surgeries such as open cholecystectomy, open appendicectomy, and hernia surgery, and for postoperative analgesia.
emphasis: A transversus abdominis plane block deposits anesthetic between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, where nerves course

rationales.a: Between 1 and 2 is not the target neurovascular plane shown.
rationales.b: Deep to layer 3 places anesthetic beyond the intended plane.
rationales.d: Superficial to layer 1 is outside the abdominal-wall nerve plane.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q006.takeaway: The section is below the arcuate line, about midway between umbilicus and pubic symphysis; posterior rectus sheath is absent there.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q006.displayText:
The section is below the arcuate line, about midway between umbilicus and pubic symphysis; posterior rectus sheath is absent there.

The image represents a transverse section through the rectus sheath below the arcuate line. The arcuate line is located midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis.

The rectus sheath is formed from the aponeuroses of external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis. Each aponeurosis is bilaminar.

Above the arcuate line: the anterior layer is formed by both leaves of external oblique and the anterior leaf of internal oblique; the posterior layer is formed by the posterior leaf of internal oblique and both leaves of transversus abdominis.

Below the arcuate line: the anterior layer is formed by aponeuroses of all three muscles; the posterior layer is deficient and rectus abdominis lies directly on transversalis fascia.
emphasis: The section is below the arcuate line, about midway between umbilicus and pubic symphysis; posterior rectus sheath is absent there

rationales.a: Above the umbilicus the posterior rectus sheath is present.
rationales.c: Between umbilicus and arcuate line is above the line, where posterior sheath remains.
rationales.d: Midway from xiphisternum to pubis is not the described arcuate-line level.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q007.takeaway: Superior epigastric artery anastomoses with inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q007.displayText:
Superior epigastric artery anastomoses with inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery.

In the rectus sheath, the superior epigastric artery anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery.

The superior epigastric artery is a branch of the internal thoracic artery. They anastomose in the rectus sheath above the level of the umbilicus.
emphasis: Superior epigastric artery anastomoses with inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery

rationales.a: Internal iliac branches do not provide the inferior epigastric artery in this anastomosis.
rationales.b: Superficial circumflex iliac is a femoral branch and does not form the paired epigastric vessel.
rationales.c: The inferior epigastric arises from external iliac, not directly from femoral artery.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q008.takeaway: The marked pyramidalis is supplied by the subcostal nerve (T12), with occasional L1 contribution.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q008.displayText:
The marked pyramidalis is supplied by the subcostal nerve (T12), with occasional L1 contribution.

The structure marked in the image is pyramidalis, supplied by the subcostal nerve (ventral ramus of T12).

Pyramidalis is a triangular muscle within the rectus sheath. Its base is attached to the anterosuperior margin of the pubis and ligamentous fibres in front of the symphysis, and its apex is attached to the linea alba.

It receives terminal branches of the subcostal nerve (T12). In some cases it may be innervated wholly or partly by fibres from L1 travelling in the subcostal or ilioinguinal nerves.
emphasis: The marked pyramidalis is supplied by the subcostal nerve (T12), with occasional L1 contribution

rationales.a: Genital genitofemoral branch supplies cremaster, not pyramidalis.
rationales.b: Femoral genitofemoral branch supplies upper anterior thigh skin.
rationales.d: T7–T11 intercostals supply upper abdominal-wall muscles, but pyramidalis is chiefly subcostal.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q009.takeaway: The inguinal canal has external oblique in its anterior wall, not in the roof and posterior wall; that statement is false.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q009.displayText:
The inguinal canal has external oblique in its anterior wall, not in the roof and posterior wall; that statement is false.

External oblique is present only in the anterior wall of the inguinal canal.

Internal oblique is present in the anterior wall in the lateral one-third (muscular fibres), roof (arched fibres), and posterior wall (as part of the conjoint tendon). Transversus abdominis is present as part of the roof and posterior wall (as the conjoint tendon).
emphasis: The inguinal canal has external oblique in its anterior wall, not in the roof and posterior wall; that statement is false

rationales.a: External-oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall throughout the canal.
rationales.b: Transversalis fascia forms the posterior wall throughout, reinforced medially by conjoint tendon.
rationales.c: Internal oblique and transversus abdominis arch over the canal as its roof.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q010.takeaway: Internal spermatic fascia derives from transversalis fascia as the spermatic cord traverses the deep ring.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q010.displayText:
Internal spermatic fascia derives from transversalis fascia as the spermatic cord traverses the deep ring.

Internal spermatic fascia is a derivative of transversalis fascia. External spermatic fascia is derived from external oblique aponeurosis, and cremasteric fascia from internal oblique.

The ilioinguinal nerve does not enter the inguinal canal at the deep ring; it enters by piercing the posterior wall. The cremasteric artery is a branch of the inferior epigastric artery. Indirect inguinal hernias occur in both men and women.
emphasis: Internal spermatic fascia derives from transversalis fascia as the spermatic cord traverses the deep ring

rationales.b: Ilioinguinal nerve enters the canal by piercing internal oblique; it does not enter through the deep ring.
rationales.c: Cremasteric artery usually arises from inferior epigastric artery, not superior epigastric.
rationales.d: Indirect inguinal hernias can occur in women, although they are less common.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q011.takeaway: Urine from a bulbar urethral rupture can track into perineum, scrotum and lower anterior abdominal wall, but not the medial thigh.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q011.displayText:
Urine from a bulbar urethral rupture can track into perineum, scrotum and lower anterior abdominal wall, but not the medial thigh.

In bulbar urethral injury, the medial portion of the thigh is the least likely site for collection of urine.

Rupture of the urethra below the urogenital diaphragm causes extravasation into the superficial perineal pouch, penis and scrotum in males or labia majora in females, and the anterior abdominal wall.

Below the umbilicus, superficial fascia divides into Camper's fatty layer and Scarpa's membranous layer. Scarpa's fascia is continuous with the membranous superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia). Colles' fascia attaches to fascia lata along Holden's line, extending laterally from the pubic tubercle; extravasated fluid cannot pass into the medial thigh below this line because of this firm attachment.
emphasis: Urine from a bulbar urethral rupture can track into perineum, scrotum and lower anterior abdominal wall, but not the medial thigh

rationales.a: Urine can spread into the superficial perineal pouch and perineum.
rationales.b: Scarpa fascia continuity can permit urine to track onto anterior abdominal wall.
rationales.d: Urine can enter scrotal/root tissues through superficial fascial continuity.

marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q012.takeaway: The conjoint tendon is structure 3, formed by fused lower aponeurotic fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
marrow__ANAT_CH47_Q012.displayText:
The conjoint tendon is structure 3, formed by fused lower aponeurotic fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

The structure marked 3 is the conjoint tendon. It is formed from the lower fibres of internal oblique and the lower part of the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis. It attaches to the pubic crest and extends variably along the pectineal line.

Transversus abdominis origin: internal surface of 7th-12th costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and connective tissue deep to the lateral third of the inguinal ligament. Insertion: linea alba with the aponeurosis of internal oblique, pubic crest, and pecten pubis via the conjoint tendon.
emphasis: The conjoint tendon is structure 3, formed by fused lower aponeurotic fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis

rationales.a: Label 1 is not the conjoint tendon according to the source diagram.
rationales.b: Label 2 marks a different inguinal-region structure; conjoint tendon is 3.
rationales.d: Label 4 is not the fused medial tendon insertion.
